claims.proposition_evaluated: The City of Edmonton removed motor-vehicle through lanes for bike lanes across a geographically broad share of Edmonton, where broad means qualifying corridors in at least 8 of the 15 district-plan areas. The alternative threshold is 5 areas.
claims.interpretation_notes: Verdict: Partially supported. City records establish specific conversions, including 102 Avenue, 121–111 Street; 83 Avenue, 99–106 Street, with the 102–104 Street exception; and 100 Street, 76–83 Avenue. The City’s route table also identifies the 2025 96 Street, 119–124 Avenue, conversion as a candidate qualifying corridor. The verified examples are concentrated in Central and the south side, rather than establishing the required spread across 8 areas; the alternative threshold of 5 is also not met on the verified evidence. I could not independently count the frozen snapshot, group every built feature into T corridors, or establish R, so I cannot give a complete census or a feature-unit recomputation. I do not treat unverified areas or missing records as evidence that no conversions occurred there. This antecedent finding says what the City did and does not answer whether congestion rose or fell, how many trips shifted, or why the City made the changes.

supporting_evidence.finding: The May 2017 fact sheet says 102 Avenue from 121 to 111 Street was a two-way road, specifies removal of the westbound travel lane to fit a protected bike lane, and states the planned one-way eastbound configuration. The City’s 2017 West Central Bike Routes guide describes the avenue as one-way eastbound.
supporting_evidence.source_title: 102 Avenue Bike Route (111–136 Street) Fact Sheet, pp. 1–2; West Central Bike Routes
supporting_evidence.source_date: May 2017 fact sheet; guide published 2017; exact publication and last-updated dates not stated
supporting_evidence.establishes: Prior through-lane use, the westbound lane removal and bike-lane rationale on 102 Avenue, 121–111 Street; the route guide corroborates the planned directional change.

supporting_evidence.finding: The City’s 2017 pre-construction display describes 83 Avenue, 99–106 Street, as a two-lane local roadway planned to become eastbound-only for cars, except 102–104 Street, with protected bike lanes. A March 2018 City display reports construction on the 95A–106 Street portion in 2016 and 2017.

supporting_evidence.establishes: Prior two-way through use and the planned conversion with protected bike lanes; the construction display corroborates completion on part of the route. The two-way section at 102–104 Street is excluded.

challenging_evidence.finding: The City’s 2021 132 Avenue options package describes variable existing lane configurations and options for making driving lanes consistent; it does not by itself establish which lane configuration was built. The final design and as-built segment must be matched to the on-street inventory before counting this corridor.
challenging_evidence.source_title: 132 Avenue Renewal: Exploring Options and Tradeoffs
challenging_evidence.source_date: April–May 2021; no separate last-updated date stated
challenging_evidence.establishes: The corridor had varying prior configurations and that options were considered; it is not proof of a completed through-lane conversion.

challenging_evidence.finding: The City describes a permanent traffic-lane reduction on 102 Avenue between 107 and 102 Street in connection with Valley Line West LRT accommodation. This is a distinct segment and does not establish a bike-lane-caused through-lane conversion east of 109 Street.
challenging_evidence.source_title: Valley Line West Final Traffic Configuration
challenging_evidence.source_date: Date not stated on retrieved page; available by September 23, 2026
challenging_evidence.establishes: A distinct LRT-related traffic-lane reduction on 102 Avenue, not the named bike-lane conversion.

limitations: I did not independently retrieve or calculate from the frozen GeoJSON snapshot. Therefore I cannot report my observed feature count, T, R, a complete corridor list, or C and A as a census. The brief gives the snapshot feature count as 3,175, but I did not independently verify it.

The City route table supports specific completed route changes, but the full inventory-matched corridor grouping and district-plan overlay have not been completed here. The verified examples establish occurrence in at least two district-plan areas; the broad threshold is not established by them.
The 96 Street entry should be matched to the frozen inventory and its prior through-lane configuration checked before including it in a final C count.

what_would_change_my_verdict: An inventory-matched City-record census establishing qualifying conversions in at least 8 district-plan areas would change the verdict to Supported; 5–7 areas would meet the alternative threshold only.
A complete City-record census showing no qualifying conversions, with prior lane use established for all built corridors, would change the verdict to Contradicted.
A complete review showing no qualifying conversions but incomplete prior-use records would change the verdict to Not established.
claims.suggested_one_line: City records establish specific through-lane conversions for bike facilities, but the verified examples do not establish that they occurred across a broad share of Edmonton’s district-plan areas.
claims.suggested_short_answer: City records show completed through-lane changes associated with bike routes on specific corridors, including 102 Avenue, 83 Avenue and 100 Street; the City also lists a 2025 conversion on 96 Street that should be matched to the frozen inventory. These examples do not establish conversions in at least eight of Edmonton’s 15 district-plan areas. The finding describes what was built and says nothing about whether congestion changed.
